mcqs.question: Why does a buggy third-party driver commonly crash the entire system on a monolithic kernel like Linux or Windows?
options: Drivers are always written in a less safe programming language than the rest of the kernel
The driver runs in kernel space with full privilege, so its bugs can corrupt kernel memory or state directly
Monolithic kernels don't support drivers at all, so this shouldn't happen
Drivers run at a lower priority than the scheduler, causing a deadlock
mcqs.explanation: In a monolithic kernel, drivers run with the same unrestricted privilege as the rest of the kernel, so a bug there can corrupt shared kernel state and bring down everything — there's no isolation boundary protecting the rest of the kernel from it. Language choice isn't the structural cause, monolithic kernels absolutely support drivers, and this isn't a priority/deadlock issue.

mcqs.question: In a microkernel design, what happens when a filesystem service running in user space crashes?
options: The entire kernel immediately panics, identically to a monolithic kernel
The kernel can restart just that service, since it's an isolated user-space process, not kernel code
All other user-space services also crash automatically
The hardware itself halts until manual intervention
mcqs.explanation: This is the core benefit of the microkernel design: because the filesystem service is an ordinary user-space process, its crash is contained, and the minimal kernel can detect and restart it without the rest of the system going down. A monolithic kernel is the one where this would panic the whole system.

mcqs.question: A team building a safety-critical automotive control system wants a guarantee that one faulty component can never crash the whole system. Which architecture best fits, even at some performance cost?
options: A traditional monolithic kernel like mainline Linux
A loadable-kernel-module-heavy design with no other changes
Whichever kernel has the fewest total lines of code
A microkernel design, accepting IPC overhead in exchange for strong fault isolation
mcqs.explanation: Microkernels trade IPC overhead specifically for strong isolation guarantees, which is exactly the property this scenario needs. A monolithic kernel or heavier module use doesn't provide that isolation, and line count alone says nothing about isolation properties.

mcqs.question: What isolation benefit do Linux loadable kernel modules (LKMs) provide compared to statically-compiled kernel code?
options: None — a buggy module can still crash the whole kernel since it runs with the same full privilege
LKMs run in a fully sandboxed user-space process
LKMs are automatically restarted by the kernel if they crash, like a microkernel service
LKMs cannot access kernel memory, only their own private memory region
mcqs.explanation: LKMs gain flexibility (load/unload without rebuilding) but not isolation — once loaded, they run with the same unrestricted kernel privilege as built-in code, so a bug there is just as dangerous as a bug in the base kernel. They don't run in user space, aren't auto-restarted, and do have full kernel memory access.

mcqs.question: What's the most accurate modern take on "microkernels are too slow to use in practice"?
options: It's still fully true today exactly as it was in the 1990s, with no meaningful change
It was a fair criticism of early implementations, but modern microkernels like seL4 have closed much of that gap and see real deployment where isolation matters
It was never true at any point in OS history
Microkernels eliminated IPC entirely, making the criticism irrelevant
mcqs.explanation: Early microkernel IPC really was a bottleneck, but modern designs (seL4 especially) have engineered and formally verified IPC paths that are fast enough for real production and safety-critical use — the historical criticism doesn't fully hold today. It also wasn't baseless originally, and microkernels didn't eliminate IPC — that's their core mechanism, not something they removed.
